leads.name: The Ash of Jardin d'Isabelle
leads.age_estimate: roughly 160 years, from a registered planting date around 1870
leads.story:
This European ash shares the Jardin d'Isabelle with the copper beech the register also lists nearby, banded to the same decade, a planting around 1870 and roughly 160 years old. Ash dieback, the fungal disease that has killed a large share of the Netherlands' ash population since around 2010, makes every surviving ash this age worth noting: a tree that has stood for a century and a half in a garden setting and made it through more than a decade of a disease that has taken down ash trees far younger.

Ash is among the last trees in a Dutch garden to come into leaf each spring and among the first to drop in autumn, leaving it bare for more than half the year, and its matt black, hoof-shaped buds are one of the easiest ways to identify it through the winter months when nothing else here carries them.

The register gives no history of the tree itself beyond species and decade, unlike its beech neighbour a few steps away, which carries an actual anecdote attached to the garden. If you know whether this ash shows any sign of dieback, or more of its history, tell us.
leads.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it in winter by its matt black, hoof-shaped buds, bare while everything else is still in leaf. It stands in the Jardin d'Isabelle, near the copper beech.

leads.name: The Sycamore of Janskamperstraat
leads.age_estimate: roughly 120 years, from a registered planting date around 1910
leads.story:
This sycamore maple grows on Janskamperstraat in Geleen, banded by the national register to a planting around 1910, roughly 120 years old. Sycamore is one of the faster-growing large maples planted across the Netherlands through the early twentieth century, valued for tolerating wind, salt and poor soil better than most other broadleaf trees, which made it a common choice for streets and windbreaks in industrial and mining towns like Geleen was becoming through this period.

At 120 years a sycamore has usually reached close to its mature size, with the broad, five-lobed leaves and winged seed pairs, the helicopters children collect every autumn, that the species produces in quantity. Its bark develops a distinctive scaly, plated pattern with age, flaking in irregular patches that can make an old sycamore look almost as textured as a plane tree from a distance.

The register records nothing about this specific tree's history beyond species and decade, which is ordinary for a street tree whose interest is simply having outlasted whatever else stood on the street around it. If you know more, tell us.

best_time.label: September to October: winged seeds that spin down in pairs

leads.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its bark, scaly and plated, flaking in irregular patches almost like a plane tree's. It stands on Janskamperstraat, Geleen.

leads.name: The Pin Oak of Sittard's Stadspark
leads.age_estimate: roughly 120 years, from a registered planting date around 1910

location.address: Stadspark, ter hoogte van Vijverweg 3, Sittard

leads.story:
This pin oak grows in Sittard's Stadspark, banded by the national register to a planting around 1910, roughly 120 years old. Pin oak is another North American import, native to wet bottomland from the Great Lakes down through the Mississippi valley, and it was planted across Dutch parks through the early twentieth century for a growth habit unlike almost any native oak: a straight central trunk holding a distinctly layered crown, upper branches reaching up, middle branches running level, and lower branches sweeping down toward the ground, sometimes low enough to brush a visitor's head.

Its leaves are the most deeply cut of any oak commonly planted in Europe, with narrow, bristle-tipped lobes that give the crown a fine, almost feathery texture from a distance, and in autumn they turn a rich bronze-red that holds on the branches, often through much of the winter, longer than most other oaks manage.

A tulip tree the register also lists grows a short walk away in the same park, so this pin oak is one stop on what could be a short walk through Stadspark's older plantings. The register records nothing further about this tree specifically. If you know more, tell us.

best_time.label: October, when the finely cut leaves turn bronze-red and hold through winter

leads.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its layered crown, lower branches sweeping down low enough to brush your head, and finely cut leaves. It stands in Sittard's Stadspark.

leads.name: The Tulip Tree of Sittard's Stadspark
leads.age_estimate: roughly 110 years, from a registered planting date around 1920

location.address: Stadspark, ter hoogte van Vijverweg 7, Sittard

leads.story:
This tulip tree grows in Sittard's Stadspark, a short walk from the pin oak the register also lists nearby, banded to a planting around 1920, roughly 110 years old. Liriodendron tulipifera comes from the eastern United States, where it grows as one of the tallest broadleaf trees in North America, and the name undersells what it actually produces: cup-shaped flowers, greenish yellow with an orange band inside, closer to a magnolia in shape than a tulip, opening from late spring high in the crown where they are easy to miss from directly underneath.

The leaves are the more reliable identifying feature, four-lobed with a flat or slightly notched tip as if squared off with scissors, unlike any native European tree, and in autumn they turn a clean, even butter yellow across the whole crown rather than the patchy colour many species manage.

A municipal park stocked with North American specimens like this one and the pin oak nearby reflects an early twentieth century fashion for filling Dutch parks with trees that had no local precedent, chosen for how unlike anything native they looked. The register records only species and decade for this one. If you know more, tell us.

best_time.label: October, when the whole crown turns a clean, even butter yellow

leads.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by leaves with a flat, squared-off tip unlike any native tree, and cup-shaped flowers high in the crown from late spring. It stands in Sittard's Stadspark.
